description:
Our team studies locations on Earth that resemble the environments of the Moon and Mars. We explore deserts, polar regions, volcanic areas and rocky landscapes to understand their similarities with other planets.

Our three-member team works together through research, scientific observation and data analysis. Our goal is to identify suitable Earth locations for studying future space exploration and permanent human bases on the Moon and Mars.
summary:
For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge (Ajmer Local Event), we developed an interactive mapping and data-analysis tool that identifies Earth locations matching the geological, environmental, and topographical conditions of permanent Moon bases and Mars.
How It Addresses the Challenge
Using open datasets from NASA Worldview and the Planetary Data System, our solution evaluates terrestrial regions—such as deserts, volcanic terrains, polar ice caps, and caves—against lunar and Martian surface criteria. Rather than relying only on visual similarity, it compares mineral composition, extreme temperatures, dust processes, and terrain suitability for robotics, construction, and resource utilization, while noting where each analog succeeds or falls short.
Why It Is Important
Testing hardware in space is costly and risky. Well-characterized Earth analogs allow NASA and mission teams to safely test rovers, habitats, navigation systems, and astronaut operations before launch. By uncovering new, scientifically validated analog sites, our project accelerates preparation for the Artemis campaign, permanent Moon bases, and future human missions to Mars.
details:
The selected topic is the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge: "Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars." This project tasks participants with discovering and analyzing places on Earth—known as terrestrial analogs—that mimic the extreme environmental and geological conditions of the Moon and Mars.

What the Project Does

• Finds Off-World Twins on Earth. The project identifies new or under-studied terrestrial locations—such as deserts, polar ice caps, volcanic fields, craters, and underground lava tubes—that share physical characteristics with future lunar bases or Martian landing sites.

• Evaluates Operational Suitability. Rather than just finding places that look like the Moon or Mars visually, the project identifies terrains capable of testing real mission hardware. This includes testing landing systems, rover mobility, autonomous navigation, habitat construction, and resource extraction.

• Defines Scientific Limits. Because no site on Earth can replicate lunar gravity, vacuum, or space radiation, the project maps out both where a terrestrial analogy holds true and where its scientific limitations begin.

How It Works

• Multi-Planet Data Cross-Referencing. Teams use open satellite and orbital datasets from the NASA Space Apps Challenge, including NASA Earthdata, Worldview, the Planetary Data System, and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) observations.

• Parameter Comparison. Researchers compare specific metrics across planets, such as surface topography, mineral composition, extreme temperature swings, sunlight angles, permafrost levels, and dust storm dynamics.

• Tool & Visualization Building. Participants process this data—often using Geographic Information Systems (GIS), similarity scoring metrics, or machine learning algorithms—to output interactive maps, comparison atlases, or analytical software tools.

Key Benefits

• Cost-Effective Mission Testing. Testing rovers, spacesuits, and drilling equipment in harsh Earth environments is vastly cheaper and safer than discovering design flaws during a live spaceflight.

• Expanded Training Grounds. While NASA already uses well-known sites like the Atacama Desert and Death Valley (featured in the NASA Planetary Analog Explorer), uncovering new sites globally gives international space agencies more accessible, diverse, and specialized testing facilities.

• Realistic Astronaut Preparation. Crews can practice living, communicating, and solving emergencies in isolated, rugged terrain that closely mirrors the psychological and physical challenges of deep-space habitats.

Overall Impact

• Accelerates the Artemis Campaign. By pinpointing Earth environments that match the lunar South Pole's lighting and icy soil, the project directly supports NASA's goal of establishing a permanent, sustainable human presence on the Moon.

• De-Risks Future Mars Exploration. Lessons learned from testing life-support systems and robotic construction in Martian analogs on Earth reduce the risk of mission failure when humans eventually travel to Mars.

• Advances Earth Science. Studying how extreme cold, aridity, and geological processes shape remote parts of Earth simultaneously improves our understanding of our own planet's climate and geology.

If you are planning to build a project for this challenge, let me know:

• Your preferred technical approach (e.g., an interactive web map, a machine learning model, or a scientific case study)

• Your target destination (Moon, Mars, or both)
